digest.top_line: RTOG 9601: 24mo bicalutamide 150mg added to salvage RT lifts 12-yr OS 76.3% vs 71.3% (HR 0.77) in pN0 post-RP pts, PSA 0.2-4.0.
digest.tldr: Prostate carried the day: RTOG 9601's OS gain from adding bicalutamide to salvage RT concentrates at entry PSA ≥0.7 (post hoc; HR 1.13 at <0.7), and focal salvage HDR for radiorecurrence (F-SHARP) posts 3-yr bPFS 62.7% with no acute G3+. Seminoma data favor smaller RT fields: Classen 6-yr RFS 95.3% (IIA); nodal mapping places 99% of nodes within a vascular CTV.

sites.intro: Two seminoma datasets back reduced RT fields for stage II disease, one with long-term outcomes, one a recurrence map only.

studies.name: Nodal metastasis mapping in seminoma (RT fields)
studies.tldr: Across 145 imaging-positive nodes in 90 pts, 99% sat within a 2.5cm lateral/posterior and 2.1cm anterior arterial expansion, smaller than Classen fields.

details.text: 🔍 Retrospective imaging-mapping series, 90 pts, 4 academic centers, diagnosed 1996-2011

details: 🔍 CS IIA/B or recurrent CS I seminoma after orchiectomy; nodes ≤5cm, no distant mets

details.text: ⚠️ Node positivity by imaging only: >1cm short axis on CT (86 pts) or nanoparticle-enhanced MRI (4 pts); not biopsy-proven

details: 📊 4 pts (4%) had pelvic-only relapse

subdetails: Left-sided: no PA nodes right of the aorta; none in renal hilum or above L1
Right-sided: 8 contralateral PA nodes (13%) in 5 (12%) pts; none above L2
Right-sided: single right renal hilar node, 3.5cm from aorta
2.5cm lateral and posterior expansion of arterial vasculature, excluding vertebral bodies
Superior border 1cm above right or 1.5cm above left renal artery, whichever is more inferior
ART for CS I: caudal border 1cm inferior to aortic bifurcation

details.text: ⚠️ 5 nodes (3.5%) in 4 pts fell outside a Classen field: 3 left inguinal, 1 renal hilar, 1 gonadal-vein
🔗 Classen field (prospective phase II, 2003) showed no relapse increase vs larger fields; this data supports its acetabular inferior border

details: ⚠️ Recurrence map, not field-failure data: no pt treated with the proposed CTV; authors restrict use to research setting

verdict.rationale: Retrospective imaging-defined node map; proposed CTV never tested for relapse or toxicity. Authors themselves limit it to research use pending validation.
verdict.audience: CS IIA/B or recurrent CS I seminoma post-orchiectomy, nodes ≤5cm

studies.significance: The superior border is the volume lever: no left-sided node sat above L1 or in the renal hilum, supporting a border 1.5cm above the left renal artery rather than T10/T11. Prior inguinal or pelvic surgery is the exception, needing an inferior border 1cm below the femoral head.
studies.monday_clinic: In CS IIA/B seminoma with a left-sided primary and no prior inguinal or scrotal surgery, this supports a vascular-referenced CTV without right paracaval or high superior extension; it does not extend to pts with prior pelvic surgery, where inguinal coverage was needed.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: **Retrospective multicenter** imaging review, 4 academic centers, staging scans read by a single abdominal radiologist. Each node transferred to a CT template by its relation to the aorta and renal arteries, with craniocaudal scaling for height.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: **90 pts**, CS IIA/B or recurrent CS I seminoma after orchiectomy, nodes ≤5cm. 40 (44%) relapsed on CS I surveillance at a median **8.5 mo** (range 3.2-50.4); 50 (56%) node-positive within 3 mo of diagnosis. 48 (53%) left-sided, 41 (46%) right-sided primaries.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: Proposed CTV: **2.5cm lateral/posterior** and **2.1cm anterior** expansion of arterial vasculature, superior border 1cm above the right or 1.5cm above the left renal artery. Classen acetabular inferior border retained; NCCN 2cm GTV boost and setup margins added on top.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: **145 nodes**, average 1.6 per pt, median size 18 mm. **99%** of nodes fell inside the proposed expansion; nodal region was unrelated to CS at presentation (P = 0.16) or primary laterality (P = 0.15).

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Classen extended fields (prospective phase II, 2003) are the NCCN- and European consensus-endorsed standard; this map supports Classen's acetabular inferior border but argues the T10/T11 superior border overtreats. MRC TE10 linked smaller fields to less acute GI toxicity and leukopenia. Martin et al. used a 1.4cm aorta/IVC expansion from non-enlarged nodal anatomy.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents infradiaphragmatic CS IIA/B or surveillance-relapse seminoma with nodes ≤5cm and no prior pelvic surgery. Does not represent CS IIC/III disease, pts with prior scrotal or inguinal surgery, or right-sided primaries with renal hilar spread.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Single-timepoint CT in many pts, so original nodal position before reaching size criteria was estimated, not observed. Two atypical nodes (1.4%) were excluded from the expansion analysis. Relapses that would emerge outside the reduced field after treatment are unmeasured.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The case for smaller fields rests on second-malignancy risk in a young cohort, with extended fields linked to **up to 50% more SMNs** than PA strip fields in cited data. The trade the authors accept is a small out-of-field relapse risk, judged salvageable, against lower SMN risk.

studies.interpretation:
The value of this series is that it replaces bony landmarks, inherited from the pre-CT era, with a target defined by where seminoma nodes actually appear relative to the aorta and renal arteries. The Classen field remains the reference standard for CS IIA/B, and the prospective phase II data behind it already established that dropping the lower pelvis from the field did not raise relapse. This paper extends the same logic upward and laterally: the observed node distribution suggests the T10/T11 superior border and the generous paracaval coverage of conventional fields treat tissue that rarely, if ever, harbors disease. For a left-sided primary, the absence of any PA node right of the aorta and any node above L1 makes the case for trimming the right-sided and cranial volume particularly direct.

The methodological caveat that should move confidence most is what the denominator represents. These are radiographically enlarged nodes, defined by a short-axis cutoff on CT in almost every pt, and many pts had a single scan. The map therefore shows where nodal disease becomes visible, not necessarily where microscopic disease sits at the moment a field is drawn. A reduced CTV built on gross relapse sites could miss subclinical spread that would never appear in this kind of dataset, and that is exactly the failure mode a recurrence map cannot detect. The two atypical right-sided nodes, at the renal hilum and along the gonadal vein, are a reminder that right-sided drainage is less predictable, and the 13% contralateral PA rate for right-sided primaries means asymmetric trimming is a left-sided argument, not a general one.

The second issue is that nothing was treated. There is no relapse rate, no dosimetric comparison and no toxicity endpoint for the proposed volume. The SMN rationale draws on Hodgkin survivor data and modeling, which supports the direction of benefit but not its size for this specific CTV. The authors are candid that the volume belongs in a research setting.

Context has also shifted since publication in 2013. The authors themselves favor surveillance for CS I, and adjuvant RT for CS I has largely receded, so the question this paper most informs is the CS IIA/B field. There, the decision it moves is volume design rather than whether to irradiate: a CT-planned, vascular-referenced CTV with a lower superior border is consistent with these data, while the exception for prior inguinal or scrotal surgery argues for extending inferiorly in that subset. What would make the proposal wrong is a prospective cohort treated to this volume showing marginal or out-of-field relapse clustering near the excluded superior or paracaval regions; until such data exist, the map is best read as a rationale for contouring choices within established field families rather than a replacement for them.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: The superior border is the volume lever: no left-sided node sat above L1 or in the renal hilum, supporting a border 1.5cm above the left renal artery rather than T10/T11. Prior inguinal or pelvic surgery is the exception, needing an inferior border 1cm below the femoral head.

open_questions: Out-of-field relapse rate when treating the vascular-based CTV prospectively
Does nanoparticle MRI identify nodes before size criteria change target volumes?

studies.name: Classen reduced-portal RT for stage IIA/B seminoma
studies.tldr: 6-yr RFS 95.3% (IIA) and 88.9% (IIB) with para-aortic/ipsilateral high iliac RT, 30/36 Gy; 100% in-field control, no late toxicity.
details: 🔍 Prospective multicentre observational study, 30 German centres, enrolled 1991-1994
🔍 N=94 enrolled, 87 assessable (7 lost to f/u, excluded); median f/u 70 mo (range 3-111)
🔍 Pure testicular seminoma, Royal Marsden stage IIA (<2 cm) or IIB (2-5 cm); elevated AFP excluded

subdetails: Para-aortic/paracaval + ipsilateral high iliac nodes, gross nodes + 2 cm margin
Upper border cranial rim T11; lower border cranial rim ipsilateral acetabulum
AP/PA opposed fields, 4-20 MV photons, 2.0 Gy/fx
IIA 30 Gy/15 fx; IIB 36 Gy; no boost

details: 📊 Patterns of failure: 100% in-field control; no pelvic, inguinal, or isolated supraclavicular relapse
📊 All 4 relapses salvaged with platinum chemo, all in continuous CR; DSS 100% both stages
📊 No grade 4 acute toxicity; late effects limited to G1 skin hyperpigmentation in 1 pt
⚠️ Protocol violations in 26 pts (29.9%), 22 major; efficacy reported as ITT
⚠️ IIB arm is only 21 pts; CI lower bound 74.4%, so IIB control estimate is imprecise
⚠️ 70-mo median f/u too short to capture second-malignancy and cardiac late effects
🔗 Source contrasts modified EP (9% relapse, 33% G3/4 leukopenia) and carboplatin alone (15% failure)

verdict.rationale: Single-arm observational cohort with no randomised comparator vs chemo; IIB subset small (n=21). Single-arm gate caps the verdict despite 70-mo follow-up.
verdict.audience: Pure seminoma, Royal Marsden stage IIA/IIB, AFP-negative, post-orchiectomy

studies.significance: Field size is the transferable parameter: dropping the contralateral pelvis and inguinal chain to a T11-to-acetabulum hockey-stick gave no pelvic or inguinal failures and 100% in-field control. 3 of 4 relapses involved the mediastinum, outside any infradiaphragmatic field, so the residual risk is systemic, not a portal or dose problem.
studies.monday_clinic: In AFP-negative stage IIA seminoma, this supports para-aortic plus ipsilateral high iliac RT to 30 Gy without pelvic or mediastinal extension; it does not settle stage IIB, where 21 pts and a 74.4% lower CI bound leave room for chemo-based approaches.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Prospective multicentre **observational** study, 30 German centres, enrolment April 1991 to March 1994. 94 enrolled, **87 assessable**, median follow-up **70 mo**. Analysed ITT, including 22 pts with major protocol violations.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Histologically confirmed **pure testicular seminoma**, Royal Marsden **stage IIA (<2 cm) or IIB (2-5 cm)** after high inguinal orchiectomy. Elevated AFP excluded; βHCG up to 200 IU/L allowed after year 1. 66 IIA, 21 IIB; median age 32.5 and 32.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: AP/PA hockey-stick to para-aortic/paracaval and **ipsilateral high iliac** nodes, gross disease plus 2 cm margin, T11 to acetabular rim. **2.0 Gy/fx: 30 Gy for IIA, 36 Gy for IIB**, no boost; 5 pts treated bilateral iliac.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: **Primary:** relapse-free survival at 5 years. **Secondary:** disease-specific survival (expected at least 95% at 5 yr) and acute/late GI and skin toxicity.

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: Acute toxicity dominated by grade 1 nausea (53% IIA, 52% IIB); **no grade 4**. **No late GI toxicity**, no peptic ulceration, no second malignancy to date; one pt with G1 skin hyperpigmentation.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Prior stage II series used larger portals covering the entire ipsilateral iliac/inguinal chain and contralateral pelvis; this cohort shows the reduced field loses no pelvic control. The source places modified EP (9% relapse, 33% G3/4 leukopenia) and carboplatin alone (15% failure) as **no better on control** with more toxicity.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents AFP-negative pure seminoma, stage IIA/IIB by Royal Marsden, treated with infradiaphragmatic RT. Does not represent bulky stage IIC+, nonseminoma, or pts unsuitable for platinum salvage.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Study was **not designed to test** reduced vs extended portals, so the toxicity advantage is inferred against historic series. Seven pts lost to follow-up were excluded rather than censored, and the IIB cohort is too small for its own protocol-violation analysis.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: Failures were all extra-field (mediastinal or lung) except one lateral para-aortic field-edge relapse, and all were salvaged, so **DSS was 100%**. The authors suggest room for dose reduction below 30 Gy in IIA, though no dose-response relationship was established.

studies.interpretation:
The value of this cohort is less the headline control rate than the target volume it validates. Stage II seminoma RT historically meant a dog-leg covering the full ipsilateral iliac and inguinal chain plus the contralateral pelvis. Here, cutting the field to para-aortic and ipsilateral high iliac nodes, with the lower border at the acetabular rim, produced no pelvic or inguinal relapse and 100% in-field control. The one marginal failure was a lateral para-aortic field-edge recurrence, which argues for careful lateral coverage of enlarged nodes rather than for any return to larger portals. For a radiation oncologist, that is the transferable finding: the reduced hockey-stick is enough for the infradiaphragmatic disease these pts carry.

The failure pattern also says something about what RT cannot fix. Three of the four relapses involved the mediastinum, and one had lung disease. No supraclavicular-only relapse occurred, so the authors argue that prophylactic mediastinal or supraclavicular fields would have helped essentially nobody while adding cardiac and haematologic cost. Residual risk after modern RT for stage II seminoma is distant, occult disease, and it was fully salvaged with platinum chemotherapy here, giving 100% disease-specific survival. That framing matters when comparing against chemotherapy-first approaches, which trade the small distant-relapse risk for systemic toxicity in every pt.

Confidence should run differently by stage. The IIA cohort (66 pts, 95.3% 6-yr RFS, lower CI bound 88.9%) is reasonably informative. The IIB cohort is 21 pts with a CI reaching down to 74.4%, wide enough to hold the higher IIB relapse rates of up to 33% that the authors cite from earlier literature. The source's claim that modified EP and single-agent carboplatin offer no control advantage rests on cross-series comparison with unnamed cohorts of different eras and staging, not on randomisation. A skeptic would also note that the study was observational with no prespecified comparator, that seven pts lost to follow-up were dropped rather than censored, and that nearly 30% had protocol deviations, though the authors report that all relapses occurred in per-protocol pts.

The toxicity read is favourable but immature for the endpoint that has driven seminoma de-escalation since: second malignancy and cardiovascular late effects. A 70-month median follow-up cannot capture radiation-associated second cancers, which the authors acknowledge. So the absence of late toxicity reported here should be read as absence of early-late GI and skin effects, not as evidence the long-term risk is low.

What this does not settle is the dose. Median doses of 30 and 36 Gy gave full in-field control, and three IIA pts treated to 26 Gy did not fail, which the authors take as a hint that de-escalation is possible. That is a hypothesis, not a finding. The decision this cohort moves is target volume for stage IIA/IIB seminoma when RT is chosen; whether RT should be chosen over chemotherapy or surgical approaches in stage IIB remains open, and this series is too small in IIB to answer it.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: The reduced hockey-stick (para-aortic plus ipsilateral high iliac, T11 to acetabulum) gave no pelvic or inguinal failures and 100% in-field control at 30 Gy (IIA) and 36 Gy (IIB). Contralateral pelvic and mediastinal coverage add toxicity without addressing the observed failure sites.
significance_by_specialty.medonc: All four relapses were mediastinal or pulmonary and every one was salvaged with platinum chemo, giving DSS 100%. In the source's framing, chemo-first options (modified EP 9% relapse, carboplatin 15% failure) add toxicity without better control, though the IIB cohort of 21 pts leaves that comparison open.

open_questions: Dose de-escalation below 30 Gy in stage IIA
RT vs chemotherapy in stage IIB seminoma

sites.intro: Salvage throughout: systemic add-on to prostate-bed RT, focal HDR re-irradiation for radiorecurrence, plus an SBRT margin audit.

studies.name: F-SHARP
studies.tldr: No acute G3+ toxicity and 3-yr bPFS 62.7% after dose-escalated focal salvage HDR (up to 30 Gy/1-2 fx) for intraprostatic radiorecurrence, N=62.
details: 🔍 Multi-institutional phase I/II, single-arm, N=62
🔍 Intraprostatic radiorecurrence (IPR) after any form of definitive RT for localized prostate cancer
💊 DE-fsHDR up to 30 Gy in 1-2 fractions: 24 pts 1 fx, 38 pts 2 fx
📊 1° objective: acute RT-related G3+ GU/GI toxicity (CTCAE v4.03): none occurred
📊 Late G3 toxicity in 2 pts (3.2%)
📊 QoL (EPIC-26, IPSS) changes did not meet MCID criteria
📐 No difference 1 vs 2 fractions across endpoints (all P > .05)
📊 GC (Veracyte transcriptome) in 31 pts: higher score associated with worse bPFS, rPFS, LRFS, MFS
📊 All pts with GC score >0.85 (n = 4) had biochemical, local and metastatic recurrence
⚠️ GC analysis covers only 31/62 pts; >0.85 cutpoint rests on n = 4
⚠️ No whole-gland or alternative salvage comparator; efficacy is single-arm

verdict.rationale: Single-arm phase I/II, N=62, toxicity primary objective; efficacy endpoints secondary and uncontrolled. GC signal from half the cohort.
verdict.audience: Intraprostatic radiorecurrence after definitive RT for localized prostate cancer

studies.significance: The single-fraction arm (24 pts) matched two fractions on every endpoint (all P > .05), making a one-visit focal salvage HDR schedule a real option. The GC tail is the second read: all 4 pts with score >0.85 recurred locally and distantly, so focal-only salvage looks like the wrong tool for them.
studies.monday_clinic: In intraprostatic radiorecurrence after definitive RT, this supports focal salvage HDR (up to 30 Gy in 1-2 fractions) as a low-toxicity local option; it does not settle management for the GC score >0.85 pt, where focal salvage alone failed in all 4.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: **Multi-institutional phase I/II**, single-arm, **N = 62**. Median follow-up **39.4 mo**.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: **Intraprostatic radiorecurrence (IPR) after any form of RT** for localized prostate cancer. GC results available in **31** pts.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: Dose-escalated focal salvage HDR, **up to 30 Gy in 1-2 fractions**. **24** pts received one fraction and **38** received two.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: **Primary:** acute RT-related G3+ GU and GI toxicity (CTCAE v4.03). Secondary: all-grade toxicity, QoL (EPIC-26, IPSS), bPFS, rPFS, LRFS, MFS and survival.

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: **No acute G3 toxicity.** Late G3 toxicity in **2 pts (3.2%)**; QoL changes did not meet MCID criteria.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Prospective salvage brachytherapy data after EBRT are sparse, with RTOG 0526 testing whole-gland salvage LDR in this setting. F-SHARP adds a focal, dose-escalated HDR approach and a genomic risk layer that prior salvage series lacked.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents pts with intraprostatic radiorecurrence after definitive RT treated with focal salvage HDR. Does not represent pts with extraprostatic or nodal recurrence, or whole-gland salvage.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: The GC analysis is restricted to **31 of 62** pts and the **>0.85** cutpoint rests on **n = 4**, so it is a descriptive tail, not a validated threshold. The 1 vs 2 fraction comparison was not randomized and is underpowered for equivalence.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: Toxicity is the settled part: focal dose escalation to 30 Gy in the re-irradiated gland produced **no acute G3** events. Durability is the open part, since bPFS at 3 yr is **62.7%** and the efficacy endpoints carry no comparator.

studies.interpretation:
The question F-SHARP answers well is whether a re-irradiated prostate tolerates focal dose escalation with HDR. The answer is clearly yes in this cohort: no acute grade 3 events, late grade 3 toxicity in 2 pts (3.2%), and QoL changes on EPIC-26 and IPSS that never crossed the minimal clinically important difference. For a radiation oncologist weighing salvage options in intraprostatic radiorecurrence, toxicity has historically been the reason to hesitate over re-treating the whole gland, and a focal target is the obvious lever to reduce it. This trial gives prospective, multi-institutional support for pulling that lever.

The efficacy read is less settled, and the design explains why. Disease control endpoints were secondary in a single-arm study powered around toxicity, so the 3-year rates (bPFS 62.7%, LRFS 73.0%, MFS 85.9%) describe this cohort rather than estimate an effect against anything. The central tension of focal salvage is that treating only the visible recurrence leaves untreated gland at risk, and an LRFS of 73.0% at 3 years is the figure a skeptic would point to. Without a whole-gland arm, it is not possible to say whether the local failures reflect out-of-field disease that whole-gland salvage would have covered or biology that no local therapy would have controlled. RTOG 0526 tested whole-gland salvage LDR in a similar post-EBRT setting, and the natural comparison between focal and whole-gland approaches remains unanswered by a randomized trial.

The fractionation finding has more practical weight than its framing suggests. Twenty-four pts received a single fraction and 38 received two, with no difference across endpoints (all P > .05). This was not a randomized comparison and is far too small to establish equivalence, but it shows that a single-implant schedule did not produce an obvious efficacy or toxicity penalty. For programs where a second implant is a real burden on pts and on the brachytherapy suite, that is a reason to consider the shorter schedule in a protocol or registry context.

The genomic classifier result is the part most likely to be overread. Higher scores tracked with worse bPFS, rPFS, LRFS and MFS among the 31 pts with results, and all 4 pts with a score above 0.85 recurred biochemically, locally and distantly. The direction is biologically coherent: a high-score recurrence after primary RT is a radioresistant, metastasis-prone phenotype, and a focal boost is unlikely to change its course. But the threshold is defined in four people within half the cohort, and the authors appropriately call GC promising and in need of further study. Read it as a hypothesis about who should be offered intensification (systemic therapy, wider salvage fields, or both) rather than a cutpoint ready for clinic.

What would make the reassuring read wrong? Selection is the main threat: pts referred for focal salvage HDR at experienced centers likely had imaging-defined, limited recurrences and good baseline function, which flatters both toxicity and control. Longer follow-up beyond the median 39.4 months also matters, since late GU toxicity after re-irradiation can emerge years out. The next step the data point toward is a trial that randomizes focal against whole-gland salvage, or stratifies by GC score to test intensification in the high-risk tail.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: Single-fraction focal salvage HDR (24 pts) performed no differently from two fractions (all P > .05), with no acute G3 toxicity at up to 30 Gy. The GC tail flags who focal salvage fails: all 4 pts with score >0.85 recurred locally and distantly, arguing against focal-only treatment in that group.

open_questions: Focal vs whole-gland salvage brachytherapy for intraprostatic radiorecurrence
Does GC-guided intensification improve outcomes in high-score pts?
Is single-fraction focal salvage HDR equivalent to two fractions?

studies.name: Prostate SBRT intra-fraction motion and margins
studies.tldr: Current 6 mm/3 mm posterior PTV margins covered IFPM in 92% of fractions. BIR-guideline margins ran from 3.3 mm laterally and posteriorly to 7.0 mm inferiorly.
details: 🔍 Retrospective single-centre audit: 20 pts, 36.25 Gy in 5 fx SBRT, no intra-fraction tracking
🔍 97 pre/post-treatment CBCT pairs; fiducial-based daily online IGRT match
📊 Averaged 3D RMS IFPM 2.5 mm (2SD 4.2 mm)
📊 Motion predominantly posterior (70%) and inferior (63%)
📊 IFPM exceeded current margins in 8 of 97 fractions, six in the posterior direction

details.text: 📊 Current clinical margins vs BIR-guideline-derived margins by direction

details: 📐 IFPM-only margins ≤3.5 mm; only 3% of fractions would have needed >6 mm in any direction
📐 Weak correlation of motion with time: posterior ρ = 0.38, inferior ρ = 0.36; mean imaging interval 9 min

details.text: 🔍 Identified causes in 4 of 6 evaluable out-of-margin fractions
subdetails: Pt movement in one further fraction

details: ⚠️ Delineation error is the largest margin component, measured on MRI-only contours, so likely an underestimate vs CT or fused MR/CT
⚠️ Excluding one outlier contour cuts the inferior margin to 5.8 mm from 7 mm
⚠️ Match error assumed negligible (31 observers) but not measured
⚠️ No toxicity or biochemical control endpoint; margin changes untested clinically

verdict.rationale: Single-centre retrospective geometric audit, n=20, no clinical outcome endpoint; proposed margin changes are untested against toxicity or biochemical control.
verdict.audience: Prostate SBRT 36.25 Gy/5 fx, fiducial CBCT IGRT, no intra-fraction tracking

studies.significance: The 7.0 mm inferior margin is driven mainly by apex delineation error on MRI-only contours, and dropping one outlier contour gives 5.8 mm. Lateral margins of 3.3 and 3.5 mm suggest room to trim. The posterior miss (6 of 97 fractions past 3 mm) sits at the rectal edge, which argues for bladder/rectal consistency or tracking rather than a wider posterior PTV.
studies.monday_clinic: In fiducial-guided 36.25 Gy/5 fx prostate SBRT delivered without intra-fraction tracking, this supports existing 6 mm/3 mm posterior margins as covering most fractions; it does not inform tracked, MR-guided, or CT-only-delineated workflows.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Retrospective single-centre audit of **97 pre/post-treatment CBCT pairs** from **20 pts**. Margins were calculated from IFPM alone and with the **updated BIR geometric uncertainty guidelines**.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: **36.25 Gy in 5 fractions** SBRT without intra-fraction tracking, with fiducial-based daily online CBCT IGRT. Current margins were **6 mm isotropic, 3 mm posterior**. Mean pre- to post-imaging interval was 9 min.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: **Primary:** magnitude and direction of IFPM and coverage by current margins. **Secondary:** margins derived from IFPM alone and from the BIR guidelines.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: Averaged 3D RMS IFPM was **2.5 mm (4.2 mm)**, mostly posterior (70%) and inferior (63%). Current margins covered **92%** of fractions, and 8 of 97 exceeded them, six posteriorly.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: The authors report RL motion above comparable CBCT series, with AP and SI comparable. A larger cited margin study (n=205) found smaller systematic errors and similar random errors.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents fiducial-matched, CBCT-verified 5 fx prostate SBRT without real-time tracking. Does not represent tracked or MR-guided delivery, or CT/fused-image delineation workflows.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Delineation error, the dominant component, came from an **MRI-only** study and is probably smaller than real CT or fused MR/CT error. Deformation was set to 0, match error was assumed rather than measured, and AP and SI were not split by direction.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The guideline-derived numbers suggest lateral margins could shrink while the inferior margin grows, but the inferior increase rests heavily on one outlier contour. The authors advise checking outcomes in current trials before changing practice, given favourable control and toxicity with existing margins.

studies.interpretation:
The useful finding here is less the motion data than where the margin actually comes from. Intra-fraction motion on its own needed no more than 3.5 mm in any direction, well inside the 6 mm isotropic envelope most fiducial-guided centres use. When the full BIR recipe is applied, the margin that moves is inferior, at 7.0 mm, and the authors attribute most of that to delineation error at the prostate apex. That component came from an MRI-only contouring exercise, and one outlier case alone shifts the inferior margin from 7 mm to 5.8 mm. So the headline case for a bigger inferior margin depends on observer variation at the apex more than on prostate motion, and the remedy it points to is contouring guidance, not a larger PTV.

The posterior direction tells a different story. Six of the eight out-of-margin fractions crossed the 3 mm posterior margin, which is exactly the edge kept tight to spare the rectum. The guideline-derived posterior margin of 3.3 mm barely differs from current practice, so the calculation does not ask for more posterior expansion. The failures look like occasional large excursions rather than a systematic shift, and where a cause could be found it was a change in bladder or rectal volume. That fits the broader logic of SBRT margins the authors set out: with rapid dose fall-off and only five fractions, systematic errors carry far more weight than random ones, while a single large random excursion in one fraction is a real but bounded dose deficit. The practical levers are preparation consistency, shorter imaging-to-beam time, or intra-fraction tracking, not a wider rectal margin.

Against the other series the authors cite, AP and SI motion are comparable, and the larger RL motion is explained by two pts. A cited cohort of 205 pts had smaller systematic and similar random errors, which suggests this centre's systematic budget may be on the generous side. The weak correlation between imaging interval and motion within a 6 to 15 min window argues that trimming a minute or two from delivery will not change much here, even though shorter treatment times reduced motion in other work.

Confidence should be tempered for three reasons beyond the small cohort. Match error was assumed negligible across 31 observers without being measured, and in SBRT a poorly spread fiducial set could produce a geometric miss this design cannot see. Deformation was set to zero. And delineation error measured on MRI alone will understate what a CT-planned or fused-image department actually incurs, which would push the systematic component, and the margin, up rather than down.

Nothing here links margin to outcome. The authors say as much: incidental dose outside the prostate may contribute to control, and current margins are paired with favourable biochemical control and toxicity. A department reading this should treat the lateral reduction and inferior expansion as hypotheses for its own audit, run on its own delineation and match error, not as a margin prescription.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: The inferior 7.0 mm BIR margin mostly reflects apex delineation error on MRI-only contours (5.8 mm without one outlier). Lateral margins of 3.3 and 3.5 mm suggest room to trim. Posterior misses (6 of 97 past 3 mm) point to bladder/rectal consistency or tracking, not a wider rectal-side PTV.

open_questions: Does a larger inferior margin change toxicity or biochemical control?
Would intra-fraction tracking eliminate posterior out-of-margin fractions?
Margins with CT or fused MR/CT delineation error measured

studies.name: RTOG 9601
studies.tldr: 12-yr OS 76.3% vs 71.3%, HR 0.77 (0.59-0.99), adding 24mo bicalutamide 150mg to salvage RT in pN0 post-RP pts with PSA 0.2-4.0.
details: 🔍 Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled; 840 randomized 1998-2003, 760 eligible analyzed
🔍 Median f/u 13 yrs among survivors; median age 65, median entry PSA 0.6 ng/ml
💊 Bicalutamide 150 mg daily × 24 mo vs placebo, started with RT
🔍 RT: 64.8 Gy/36 fx (1.8 Gy) to prostate bed + membranous urethra; no pelvic nodes (all pN0)

details.text: 📊 12-yr outcomes, RT + bicalutamide vs RT + placebo
📊 12-yr OS by PSA at trial entry (post hoc; PSA the only significant interaction)

details: ⚠️ Median entry PSA 0.6, so the no-benefit stratum (<0.7) is the majority of the trial

subdetails: Gynecomastia any grade 69.7% vs 10.9% (P<0.001), no prophylaxis allowed
No between-group difference in early urinary, bowel, or hematologic reactions

details: ⚠️ Bicalutamide 150 mg superseded by GnRH agonists; ADT equivalence not tested here
⚠️ Staging CT + bone scan only; RT QA showed 4.4% unacceptable variation
📐 Absolute OS difference 5.0 points; NNT 20 to avoid one death over 12 yrs

verdict.rationale: Double-blind placebo-controlled RCT, OS primary met at 13y median f/u. Benefit concentrated at PSA ≥0.7 (post hoc); bicalutamide 150mg since superseded by GnRH agonists.
verdict.audience: pN0 pT2 R1/pT3 post-RP, detectable PSA 0.2-4.0 ng/ml, salvage RT

studies.significance: The benefit follows pre-SRT PSA: 12-yr OS HR 0.45 (0.25-0.81) above 1.5 ng/ml and 0.61 at 0.7-1.5, but HR 1.13 (0.77-1.65) below 0.7, where the median entry PSA of 0.6 sat. RT was prostate bed only, 64.8 Gy/36 fx, so this informs hormone addition separately from the pelvic nodal coverage decision.
studies.monday_clinic: In a pN0 man after RP heading to salvage RT with PSA above 0.7 ng/ml, this supports adding hormone therapy to bed RT; it does not extend to PSA below 0.7 ng/ml, where the post hoc OS HR was 1.13.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: **Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled** NRG/RTOG trial; 840 randomized 1998-2003, **760 eligible** analyzed (384 vs 376). Median follow-up **13 years** among survivors.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Post-RP with lymphadenectomy, **pT2 with positive margin or pT3, pN0**, detectable PSA **0.2-4.0 ng/ml** at least 8 weeks after surgery. No prior RT or chemo; prior hormones limited to short preoperative courses (6.4%). Staging by CT and bone scan.

analysis_sections.label: Regimen
analysis_sections.body: **Bicalutamide 150 mg daily for 24 months** vs placebo, starting with RT. Adherence ≥18 months was 69.8% vs 74.7%.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: **64.8 Gy in 36 fractions of 1.8 Gy** to the prostatic bed and membranous urethra, 6-10 MV photons, 2D or 3D planning. **Pelvic nodes omitted** because all dissections were negative. QA: 64.8% per protocol, 4.4% unacceptable variation.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: **Primary: overall survival.** Secondary: disease-specific death, distant metastases, local progression, non-disease-specific death, second biochemical recurrence, AEs.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: Primary met; every disease-control endpoint favored bicalutamide (table). The OS gain is concentrated at entry PSA ≥0.7 ng/ml in post hoc subgroups.

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: **Gynecomastia 69.7% vs 10.9%**. Late GU G3 7.0% vs 6.0%; no excess early bladder, bowel or hematologic toxicity, and no excess non-disease-specific death.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: SPPORT and RADICALS-HD tested GnRH-based ADT with salvage RT, but neither used a placebo-controlled OS design. The Early Prostate Cancer Program trials of the same drug and dose reported a matching gynecomastia signal (68% vs 8%).

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents pN0 men after RP with a detectable PSA up to 4.0 ng/ml receiving prostate-bed salvage RT. Does not represent PSMA-staged, node-positive, or very-low-PSA early salvage pts, or GnRH-agonist regimens.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Post-randomization exclusion of 79 ineligible pts departs from strict ITT. Cardiac events were captured only as reported AEs, which risks ascertainment bias. Pre-PSMA staging leaves occult extra-field disease in the cohort.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: OS benefit is real but **risk-adapted**: below PSA 0.7 the subgroup trended the other way. The open questions are whether a modern GnRH agonist reproduces the effect and which duration is enough.

studies.interpretation:
This is the trial that justified hormone therapy alongside salvage RT, and its weight comes from the endpoint. A double-blind, placebo-controlled design with 13 years of median follow-up and overall survival as the primary is rare in the postoperative setting, and OS HR 0.77 met that bar. The disease-specific endpoints move the same way with larger relative effects (death from prostate cancer HR 0.49, metastases HR 0.63), with no excess non-disease-specific death, so the survival signal is hard to dismiss as chance.

The harder question is whom the average effect describes. Median entry PSA was 0.6 ng/ml, and the post hoc forest plot shows no OS benefit below 0.7 ng/ml (HR 1.13, 0.77-1.65). The effect sits at 0.7-1.5 ng/ml (HR 0.61) and above 1.5 ng/ml (HR 0.45), and PSA was the only factor with a significant interaction. When the 53.3% of pts who entered below 0.7 trend toward no benefit, the headline is telling the reader that hormone therapy at salvage depends on risk and is not a uniform add-on. Modern referral patterns make this sharper: pts now reach salvage RT at lower PSA than in this era, which moves the typical candidate toward the stratum that did not benefit.

Two features of the regimen limit direct transfer. Bicalutamide 150 mg is not what most clinics now give, and the authors acknowledge GnRH agonists replaced it. With no prophylaxis, the gynecomastia rate of 69.7% is a toxicity profile few would accept routinely. Whether two years of GnRH-agonist ADT reproduces the survival effect, or a shorter course is enough, is outside what this trial tested. GETUG-AFU 16 and SPPORT are the natural comparators for short-term GnRH-based therapy with salvage RT, and RADICALS-HD addressed duration. None of them repeats the placebo-controlled OS design, which is why this trial is still the anchor even though its drug is obsolete.

For an RT reader, the radiotherapy arm belongs to its era: 64.8 Gy in 1.8 Gy fractions to the bed alone, 2D or 3D planning, staging by CT and bone scan, pelvic nodes deliberately untreated after negative dissection. The placebo arm's 67.9% second biochemical recurrence at 12 years shows how often bed-only RT at this dose failed. A PSMA-staged population would reveal some of that failure before RT, so part of the bicalutamide effect may reflect treatment of occult disease outside the field. A modern nodal field or PET selection could absorb some of it. That would shrink the absolute benefit without necessarily reversing its direction.

What could make the headline wrong? Excluding 79 ineligible pts after randomization departs from strict intention-to-treat, though the arms stayed balanced. Cardiac events were collected only as adverse events. Neither is large enough to overturn a placebo-controlled survival result. Both argue for reading the 5.0-point absolute OS gain and the NNT of 20 as upper-end estimates for today's lower-risk, better-staged salvage population, not as a number that transfers unchanged.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: Entry PSA gates the hormone add-on to prostate-bed salvage RT: OS HR 0.45 above 1.5 ng/ml, 0.61 at 0.7-1.5, 1.13 below 0.7. RT was 64.8 Gy/36 fx with nodes omitted in pN0 pts, so the trial leaves the elective pelvic nodal question open.
significance_by_specialty.medonc: The drug tested, bicalutamide 150 mg for 24 months, is no longer standard, and gynecomastia reached 69.7% without prophylaxis. Whether GnRH-agonist ADT or a shorter course reproduces the OS HR 0.77 was not tested; the benefit concentrates at entry PSA ≥0.7 ng/ml.

open_questions: Does GnRH-agonist ADT reproduce the bicalutamide OS benefit?
Optimal hormone duration with salvage RT at low PSA
Does PSMA PET staging change who benefits from added hormones?

papers.title: Dose-Escalated Focal Salvage High-Dose-Rate Brachytherapy and Genomic Classifier Risk Stratification in Radiorecurrent Prostate Cancer: The F-SHARP Phase I/II Clinical Trial
papers.abstract: Purpose Prospective data on the management of intraprostatic radiorecurrence (IPR) after definitive radiotherapy (RT) and use of genomic classifiers (GC) in this setting are limited. We hypothesized that dose-escalated focal salvage high-dose-rate brachytherapy (DE-fsHDR) would be safe and effective, and that GC would risk stratify patients who may benefit from treatment intensification. Methods F-SHARP is a multi-institutional phase I/II trial of DE-fsHDR for IPR after any form of RT for localized prostate cancer. Patients received up to 30 Gy in 1-2 fractions. The primary objective was to determine the acute RT-related grade ≥3 CTCAE v4.03 genitourinary and GI toxicity rates. Secondary end points included all-grade toxicity, quality of life (QoL; EPIC-26 and International Prostate Symptom Score), disease control, and survival. GC analysis used a clinical-grade transcriptome assay (Veracyte, San Diego, CA). Time-to-event outcomes included biochemical progression-free survival (bPFS), radiographic progression-free survival (rPFS), local recurrence-free survival (LRFS), and metastasis-free survival (MFS). Results Twenty-four participants received one fraction and 38 received two fractions (N = 62). The median follow-up was 39.4 months. No acute grade 3 toxicities occurred. Two patients (3.2%) had late grade 3 toxicity. QoL changes did not meet criteria for a minimal clinically important difference. Three-year survival rates were 62.7% (bPFS), 67.5% (rPFS), 73.0% (LRFS), and 85.9% (MFS); there were no differences between fractionation groups (all P > .05). Among 31 patients with GC results, higher scores were associated with worse bPFS, rPFS, LRFS, and MFS. All patients with GC score >0.85 (n = 4) experienced biochemical, local, and metastatic recurrence. Conclusion DE-fsHDR is a safe and effective salvage treatment for IPR. GC score is a promising prognostic tool in patients undergoing salvage local therapy for IPR and warrants further study to guide treatment intensification.

papers.title: Mapping patterns of nodal metastases in seminoma: Rethinking radiotherapy fields
Radiotherapy for Stages IIA/B Testicular Seminoma: Final Report of a Prospective Multicenter Clinical Trial
papers.abstract: Purpose: A prospective multicenter trial was initiated to evaluate the role of modern radiotherapy with reduced treatment portals for stage IIA and IIB testicular seminoma. Patients and Methods: Patients with stages IIA/B disease (Royal Marsden classification) were assessable for the trial. Staging comprised computed tomography of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis as well as analysis of tumor markers alpha-fetoprotein and beta human chorionic gonadotropin. Linac-based radiotherapy was delivered to para-aortic and high ipsilateral iliac lymph nodes. The total doses were 30 Gy for stage IIA and 36 Gy for stage IIB disease. Results: Between April 1991 and March 1994, 94 patients were enrolled for the trial by 30 participating centers throughout Germany. Seven patients were lost to follow-up. Median time to follow-up of 87 assessable patients was 70 months. There were 66 stage IIA and 21 stage IIB patients. One mediastinal and one field-edge relapse were observed in the stage IIA group. In the stage IIB group, there was one mediastinal and one mediastinal/pulmonary relapse. All patients were treated with a salvage regimen of platinum-based chemotherapy. Actuarial relapse-free survival at 6 years was 95.3% (95% confidence interval [CI], 88.9% to 100%) and 88.9% (95% CI, 74.4% to 100%) for stage IIA and IIB groups, respectively. Maximum acute side effects were 8% grade 3 nausea for stage IIA and 10% grade 3 nausea and diarrhea for stage IIB groups. No late toxicity was observed. Conclusion: Radiotherapy for stages IIA/B seminoma with reduced portals yields excellent tumor control at a low rate of acute toxicity and no late toxicity, which supports the role of radiotherapy as the first treatment choice for these patients.

papers.title: Prostate stereotactic body radiotherapy: quantifying intra-fraction motion and calculating margins using the new BIR geometric uncertainties in daily online IGRT recommendations
papers.abstract: Objectives: To measure the magnitude of intra-fraction prostate motion (IFPM) during stereotactic radiotherapy (SBRT) delivered without intra-fraction tracking. To assess if current margins adequately cover IFPM. To derive margins using new guidelines. Methods: IFPM was determined in 20 patients receiving 36.25 Gy in 5 fractions using 97 pairs of pre- and post-treatment cone beam CT (CBCT) scans. Correlation of time between CBCT acquisitions and motion was determined. The magnitude of IFPM was compared to current margins (6 mm isotropic, 3 mm posterior). Margins were calculated using IFPM alone and updated guidelines. Results: The averaged 3D root mean square IFPM was 2.5 mm (4.2 mm). Independent prostate motion was predominantly posterior (70%) and inferior (63%). There was weak correlation between posterior (ρ = 0.38) and inferior (ρ = 0.36) IFPM and time. IFPM greater than current margins occurred in 8 of 97 fractions, six in the posterior direction. Margins were ≤3.5 mm using IFPM alone and ≤3.3 mm Left 3.5 mm Right, 7.0 mm inferior, 3.7 mm superior, 4.4 mm anterior and 3.3 mm posterior using new guidelines, compensating for motion in 92% of fractions. Conclusions: Our current SBRT margins account for 92% of IFPM, predominantly posterior and inferior. Although updated guidelines suggest an increase in margins inferiorly, any increase must be balanced against the possibility of increased toxicity, particularly if biochemical control and side-effects are favourable with current practice. Advances in knowledge: The difference between current clinical margins and those determined using updated guidance is demonstrated. The implications must be considered against clinical outcomes.
